title: The Complexity Analyzer
description: How the built-in Complexity Analyzer reads your blocks and reports Time and Space Big-O -- and how to act on what it tells you.

sections.title: Introduction to Scalability
sections.content: Code that's fine for 10 items can time out at 10,000. Writing correct output isn't enough -- you need to know how the work scales as input grows.

subsections.title: The Complexity Tab
subsections.content: The workspace's Complexity tab automatically analyzes your blocks and reports two numbers in Big-O: **Time Complexity** (how operations scale) and **Space Complexity** (how memory use scales).

subsections.title: The Complexity Graph
subsections.content: Below the scores, the Complexity Graph plots the theoretical Big-O curve for your logic -- not a live execution trace. An O(n²) result shows a steep curve, making it easy to see how badly performance degrades at scale.

sections.title: Understanding Time Complexity
sections.content: Time complexity measures how the number of operations grows with input size `n` -- worst case, constants dropped, focused purely on the trend.

subsections.title: Standard Time Complexities
bullets: **O(1) Constant:** fixed work no matter the input -- e.g. a formula, or an index lookup.
**O(n) Linear:** work scales 1-to-1 with input -- e.g. one loop through a dataset.
**O(n²) Quadratic:** scales with the square of the input -- e.g. a loop nested inside a loop.
**O(log n) Logarithmic:** the dataset shrinks each step -- e.g. Binary Search.

subsections.title: Visualizing Quadratic Growth
subsections.content: Picture every node in a network talking to every other node: 5 nodes → 25 interactions. Build a nested loop in the workspace and the Complexity Graph shows that same compounding cost immediately.

sections.title: Understanding Space Complexity
sections.content: Space complexity measures the extra memory your algorithm needs to run -- managing it well is a mark of solid design.

subsections.title: Allocation versus Mutation
subsections.content: Appending to an array as input grows requests new memory each time -- that's **O(n) Space**. Updating an existing variable or swapping values in place needs no new memory -- that's **O(1) Space**.

subsections.title: The Big O Reference Modal
subsections.content: The **Big O Reference** button in the footer opens a reference table of every complexity class, with definitions, examples, and graphs.

subsections.title: Resolving Algorithmic Bottlenecks
subsections.content: A bottleneck is the one piece of logic dragging down your whole algorithm. Summing a sequence with a loop is O(n) -- swapping in a closed-form formula instead collapses that to O(1).

sections.title: Lesson Summary
sections.content: The analyzer turns block structure directly into a scalability verdict. Optimizing means watching both Time and Space, not just one.

subsections.title: Analytical Workflow
bullets: 1. Build your logic on the canvas.
2. Open the Complexity tab to see the Big-O verdict.
3. Check the growth curve on the Complexity Graph.
4. If it's steep (e.g. O(n²)), isolate and refactor the nested logic.
5. Check the Big O Reference table for a faster alternative.
